text: Hi, everyone.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I'm Irina, former engineer at Microsoft and Supercell, and today I want to talk about auto research in a multi-agent AI village.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I will use a video game like AI village as a running example here, but the broader question is one I think many AI engineers are starting to run into.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: How do we evaluate and improve agents that carry state over a long period of time?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Before I get into the auto-research layer, I want to talk a bit about Project Paradox.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We developed Project Paradox at Supercell's AI Innovation Lab.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Me and my teammate Arnachala Manikhandan.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We built a modular AI framework that allows any developer to plug in intelligent, autonomous agents within a video game that can interact, compete, or cooperate with other players or agents as well and make them into dynamic game companions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, to give examples of what these agents can do,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The agents can move with intent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They can go to any location or person, and they're guided by their own memories, emotion, or curiosity.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: These agents can interact with the world.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They can pick up objects, drop them anywhere, and they're also aware about the context in their own environment, such as objects or other characters or agents as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I would also like to note that game developers can also add new actions for these agents to accomplish within our framework as well, instead of just dropping or placing objects.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Agents can also obviously react to what's happening around them.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And these events that happen around them affect their own beliefs and emotions on the fly as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And of course, it wouldn't be complete if agents can't start conversations, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Agents can, in this scenario, approach other agents or even the player as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this makes the game feel more alive.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And of course, these conversations are stored within their memory and is according to their own and affect their own emotions and beliefs or goals as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And altogether, these agents make our multi-agentic framework.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Yeah.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Yeah.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: One second.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the architecture was intentionally stateful behind this.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The first important part was per-agent memory.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Each agent has its own memory namespace backed by RAG, so memory did not bleed between agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Second, we tracked emotion as a small vector.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So after an event or conversation, the system could update values like joy, sadness, fear, anger, or disgust.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Third, agents had belief scores towards other agents and the player.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can think of this as a trust matrix, basically.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Like, after the interaction happens, the LLM basically decides whether the trust score should go up, down, or whether it shouldn't change at all.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And fourth, every memory receives an important score.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: To explain this better, like, let's say you had dinner a few days ago.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You probably won't remember what you had for dinner, right?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If someone was murdered a few days ago, you definitely remember that.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the agent will evaluate or the LM will evaluate an important score of an event, and if it crosses a threshold, it will store that specific memory in a separate cache so that important context can be retrieved better later on.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And here's an example of it just working.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We were going to ask one of the characters to go on a picnic with us.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Here, our character, Blossom, decides to pick up a pastry and go to the picnic area because we asked her to do so.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Keep in mind, during the conversation in the background, she plans all of these sequences of actions to accomplish, and when we talk to her afterwards, she will also reply within context as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But this is where an interesting problem actually started.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: As you saw in the last example, for short-term gameplay, our architecture worked pretty well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Like a character could make a plan, move around, talk, and remember the recent interaction and respond to us or other characters as well.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But over longer horizons, this is where we notice the social consistencies start to get weaker.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So in this example, we have one agent spreading a rumor about a sale on mangoes to another agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And that agent receives that information and goes and tells another agent about it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Later on, after a number of events occurred in between, when the player asks one of the agents about the mangoes, it doesn't exactly store that context that we were expecting, or it doesn't give us the context that we kind of want it to.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is where things are starting to get messy, naturally.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Like, the system may remember the rough topic but lose the source of the topic.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A rumor may become certain instead of just a rumor.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Like, the agent might state it as a fact.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Or an agent might know a fact but fail to remember it while creating a plan for its actions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the question here became, how do we improve a multi-agentic system over long-running social behavior and not just over one response?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is where we wanted to bring in auto-research.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: As you all know, a few months ago, Karpathy posted auto-research, and this made us immediately very curious.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Perhaps we can make the system run experiments on itself, and can we use this for our system as well?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So what we understood is instead of manually tuning a prompt or watching one nice demo, we could define a scenario suit, run the agents, collect traces, score the behavior, and change a small policy surface and only keep the changes that actually improve the score.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is where we're trying to bridge project paradox with auto research.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So at this point, basically, our multi-agency framework project paradox is more like a lab bench, and auto-research becomes the experimental loop around it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And importantly, this is not only about improving RAG retrieval.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The broader framing is optimizing the agent protocol, like how do agents write memories, retrieve them, communicate uncertainty, update trust, attribute sources, and replan around
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: new facts, basically.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Yeah.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In this context...
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Oh, yeah.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In this context, art research is not another agent in the village, like I said.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It's a meta-system outside the village.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The villagers have local perspectives, of course.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They only know what they saw, heard, remembered, or inferred.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Because there isn't a common memory database in between them, information only travels once other agents communicate them properly.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The auto research layer has a different job here.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It reads the full traces of a run, compares what happens against the scenario ground truth, scores the behavior, and proposes a constrained
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Change to the agent protocol or cognitive policy.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then it reruns the scenario and asks society-level behavior, like, did society-level behavior get better?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is the key shift we were trying to look for.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we were no longer evaluating one answer, we were evaluating an entire run.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is what one of the loops would look like.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First, we define a controlled scenario, which I'll elaborate a bit more about later.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For example, one agent learns a public fact or one agent hears a rumor.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That could be a controlled scenario.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then we run the simulation.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: During the run, we collect structured traces, observations, conversations, memory writes, retrievals, belief updates.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Whatever is relevant to us in that case, we collect.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then we score this behavior.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Did the information spread as we expected it to?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Did the source attribution survive, such as does the agent remember who started the rumor?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Did uncertainty stay uncertain?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Did agents act on what they actually knew?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then the auto-research layer here proposes a small policy change.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is important.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It should not rewrite the whole application, of course.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It should only edit a controlled policy surface.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And then we rerun.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If the score improves and the guardrails hold, we keep the improvement.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And if not, we simply just revert back.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And talking about controlled scenarios, the reason why scenario design matters is that social behavior is otherwise a bit fuzzy in general.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In the sense, if you just let the agents in an environment wander around,
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It might look cool and you might get nice interactions, but it's actually very hard to evaluate on whether the system actually improved.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So this is why we believe you need controlled scenarios.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For example, one scenario could test a public fact diffusion.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Let's say agent A learns the bakery will close tomorrow.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Do the right agents learn it?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Do they remember who said what?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Do they change their plans based on this fact?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Another scenario could test rumor uncertainty.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Let's say Agent A hears that Agent C might leave the village.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When this rumor spreads, does might leave suddenly become is leaving or does it stay as might leave?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Like does it become a fact or does it still stay as a rumor?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Another scenario could test replanning.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The group has a plan, but one agent learns, let's say, the route they wanted to take is blocked.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Do agents update this and communicate this with each other to avoid improper plan or scale actions?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The point is not that these exact scenarios are universal here.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The point we're trying to make is that long-horizon agent behavior needs scenario suits.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And talking about our Mango example again, after running one of our auto-research loops, this time after
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A long period of time when the player finally asked one of the agents about the sale on mangos, we did find that the agent was able to respond within context this time, like compared to last time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And for this talk, the exact formula we believe is less important than the shape of the scorecard.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You do not want a single vague metric like agent quality.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This will hide all the interesting failures.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Instead, you want a balanced scorecard.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For diffusion, you might measure reach.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Like how many agents know the fact after N steps.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For provenance, you measure source retention among agents who know it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: How many remember it, where it came from, et cetera.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For rumors, you can measure uncertainty preservation and false certainty rate.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For planning, you can measure action consistency and time to re-plan.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And for privacy, you can measure containment.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This matters because optimizing only one metric can create bad behavior, because let's say if you only optimize for diffusion, the agents may learn to overshare everything, and let's say if you only optimize for memory recall, you might create noisy or stale-like memories.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So, this scorecard is what keeps the system honest and prevents the auto-research agent from gamifying the system to just increase one specific score.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The other important engineering lesson that we learned over this project is that it's important to keep the editable surface really small.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The auto-research layer should not have permission to randomly rewrite the whole code base.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Instead, it's really important to freeze the harness, the scenarios, and the metrics.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we're only exposing the part of the system that we actually want to optimize here.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In Project Paradox, for us, that meant things like memory writing policy, retrieval policy, communication prompt, belief, trust rules, source attribution, planning triggers, et cetera.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This gives the search process room to improve behavior, but it also prevents it from gaming the evaluation directly, as we mentioned before.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is the difference between the LM writing random patches versus the LM actually searching within a controlled policy space.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And here are examples of the kind of changes I want this kind of loop to search over.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If source attribution disappears, the policy change might preserve source in memory rights and summaries.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If rumors harden into facts, the policy change might be store confidence, mark first-hand versus second-hand, and require hedging when retelling uncertain claims.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If public facts stay local, the policy change might classify useful public facts differently and make agents proactively share important source evidence.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The key is that these are small changes to the agent protocol, but they can have larger effects on a society-level behavior for multi-agentic systems.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This is also where I kind of want to be careful about our claims here because we believe without repeated current loop results, like I wouldn't say the system just generally improved.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We're trying to say this is the right kind of surface to expose to an auto-research layer loop because it is small enough to control, but it's still rich enough to change the social behavior to some extent at least.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the biggest lesson for me, perhaps, was that memory is not enough here.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You can add a RAG memory to an agent and still not get the current long-term horizon behavior that you were looking for.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Because agents need to sometimes know where that information came from.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: You need to preserve whether it was first-hand, second-hand, verified, or uncertain.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Sometimes you need to separate raw episodic memories from what the agent currently believes, too, and you need to test behavior through scenarios, not just through vibes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the other lesson is that rollback also is not optional.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: When you optimize social behavior, a change can improve one thing and damage another.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So a policy that spreads public facts faster might also leak private information.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A policy that increases recall might increase stale memory usage.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So the loop should basically be like a ratchet.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Try a change, score it, keep it only if the scorecard improves and guardrails whole.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And we definitely believe this is not only relevant for game agents, because although I gave you an example of using a game village, we believe, like, let's say, for example, support agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Support agents need to know which policy update comes from where and whether it supersedes an older answer.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Personal assistants, for example, need to remember commitments that they previously made.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Make corrections if the user wants to change those personal commitments.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Research agents need provenance, citations, contradiction handling, and hypothesis updates.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Coding agents need long-running context across issues, files, teammates, and changing requirements.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Workflow agents need access controls, handoffs, and replanning when the world changes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: All of these systems have the same underlying problem.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They maintain state over time, and that state affects future action.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So, they need control scenarios and behavioral scorecards is what we are proposing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So, again, in brief, a recipe for long horizon agents.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If there's one practical recipe I want you to take away, freeze the harness, define scenarios, log traces, score behavior, and expose only a small policy surface.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Search over these changes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Keep only changes that survive your measurement.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And this is an engineering pattern that we believe would make sense.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For long-running agents, the real question we believe is, across controlled runs, does the system behave better?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: To close, Project Paradox started as an attempt to make game agents feel alive in a 3D world, but the deeper engineering problem was not animation or dialogue for us.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It was the state, such as...
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Which agent knows what?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Which agent told whom?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What is true, uncertain, or outdated?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And do agents act on what they remember?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Autor research gave us a way to approach this a bit more systematically, not by trusting one demo and not by endlessly hand-tuning prompts, but by running control experiments and keeping only the changes that survived our measurement.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Long horizon agents need experiments and not just prompts, and I hope that's the takeaway that you get from this talk.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And yes, please do connect with us.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We'd love to talk if you have any questions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Thank you so much for listening.
